summary: An experimental document that defines the basic mechanisms of Photuris, a session-key management protocol used to set up shared secret keys between two parties.

plainLanguage.summary: Photuris lets two peers establish session keys without sending those keys across the network. They first exchange cookies, then values used to derive a shared secret, and finally identify and authenticate each other before setting up security parameters.

questions: what is a photuris cookie exchange
subtitle: A phased exchange for establishing session keys and security parameters between two peers.

tldr.problem: Two peers need short-lived session keys and agreed security settings without sending the resulting keys across the network.
tldr.mechanism: Photuris uses cookies, exchanged public values, identity checks, and protected messages to establish a shared secret and directional session keys.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the basic Photuris mechanisms as an Experimental protocol intended for use with IP security protocols.

today: RFC 2522 is Experimental and defines the basic Photuris session-key management mechanisms.

sections.title: Four Phases of a Key Exchange
sections.content:
Photuris establishes short-lived session keys between two parties and is intended to support IP security protocols. It begins with cookies, which help prevent simple flooding using false source addresses or ports.

The peers then exchange public values to calculate a shared secret, identify and authenticate each other, and derive separate session keys for traffic in each direction. Later messages can change keys or create revised security parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: Photuris uses a sequence of exchanges to create keys at both ends without sending the final keys over the network. Identity checks happen before the peers use the resulting security settings.

sections.title: Cookies, Values, and Identity
sections.content:
The initiator sends a cookie request, and the responder returns its own cookie and a list of supported exchange schemes. The responder does not create additional exchange state at this point.

Next, the peers select an exchange scheme and send values used to calculate their shared secret. In the identification exchange, each party identifies itself and checks the integrity of earlier values. The messages are masked using a privacy key derived from the shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Cookies let the responder answer a request before keeping exchange state. The peers then exchange values, derive the same secret, and use it to protect their identity messages.

sections.title: Security Parameters and Updates
sections.content:
A Security Parameters Index (SPI) identifies a set of one-way security settings for traffic to a destination, such as transforms and session keys. The destination-side SPI owner assigns the SPI, and the sender selects which available SPI to use for each datagram.

Photuris can exchange SPI updates to create, modify, or delete these settings. Exchange state and individual SPI state have separate lifetimes, so replacing exchange values does not automatically interrupt still-valid SPIs.
sections.plainLanguage: An SPI points to the security settings for traffic in one direction. Peers can update those settings over time, and existing settings can remain valid while a new exchange takes place.

sections.title: Randomness and Experimental Status
sections.content:
The security of Photuris depends critically on each peer generating strong secret random numbers. The RFC warns that a poor random-number generator at either end can compromise the shared secret.

The protocol includes error messages and rules for rejecting invalid or defective exchange values. RFC 2522 is Experimental and defines the basic mechanisms; it does not specify every service or application interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Photuris depends on unpredictable secret values at both peers. Weak random values can expose the shared secret, so the protocol's security depends on their quality.
